issues.legal_issue: A maintenance holding forming part of a Saranjam may be resumed and freshly granted by the government, and an adoption made without government sanction does not divest the resulting grant.
material_facts: The properties were maintenance holdings within a Saranjam and were treated by the government and the family as part of that Saranjam.
After the holder died, the government directed that the holdings be continued to his undivided brother, with effect from the holder’s death.
The widow adopted a son before the government issued that direction, but had not obtained government sanction for the adoption.
issues.conclusion: The government’s direction amounted to a valid resumption and fresh grant to the brother. The later government order was not invalidated by the adoption, and the adopted son could not claim the properties under the Saranjam Rules.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rules 1, 2 and 5 of the Saranjam Rules, a Saranjam is held as a life estate, is ordinarily resumed on the holder’s death, and may then be freshly granted by the government. The sovereign power may grant or withhold a Saranjam, and private rights cannot fetter that power. The Court relied on Daulatrao Malojirao v. Province of Bombay, which discussed Shekh Sultan Sani v. Shekh Ajmodin and Raghojirao v. Laxmanrao.

rule.if: saranjam_property_appeal and maintenance_holding_part_of_saranjam and government_freshly_granted_holding_to_another_person and adoption_lacked_government_sanction

predicates.saranjam_property_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a claim to property held as part of a Saranjam.
predicates.maintenance_holding_part_of_saranjam: The claimed property was assigned as a maintenance holding within a Saranjam.
predicates.government_freshly_granted_holding_to_an: After the prior holder died, the government resumed the holding and granted it to another person.
predicates.adoption_lacked_government_sanction: The claimant’s adoption was made without the government’s sanction.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a maintenance holding within a Saranjam that the government freshly grants to another person, an adoption made without government sanction does not entitle the adopted claimant to the property.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant relying on a family custom must plead and prove the custom’s existence and scope, and cannot obtain relief on a new theory of divestiture first advanced in appeal.
material_facts: The claimant relied on a family custom of descent by lineal primogeniture, which the other parties disputed.
The trial court found the custom unproved, and the record identified no evidence establishing it.
The claimant had not pleaded that property which had devolved on another family member under the asserted custom would be divested by a later adoption.
The claimant sought to rely in appeal on the proposition that ordinary Hindu law would divest property on a subsequent adoption.
issues.conclusion: The claimant failed to plead or prove a family custom that gave him title to the properties, and could not make out a new case of divestiture for the first time in appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A party relying on a family custom different from ordinary Hindu law must plead and prove the custom, including its precise extent and the extent to which it displaces ordinary law. A party may not make out a new case for the first time in appeal. The claimant also had to establish that the asserted custom bound the government in respect of a maintenance grant forming part of a Saranjam.

predicates.custom_based_title_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in which the claimant seeks title based on a family custom.
predicates.family_custom_not_proved: The claimant did not establish the existence and scope of the asserted family custom with evidence.
predicates.divestiture_theory_not_pleaded_at_trial: The claimant did not plead at trial that the asserted custom or a later adoption divested property that had already devolved on another person.

issues.definition: A custom-based title claim fails when the claimant appeals without proving the custom and relies on a divestiture theory that was not pleaded at trial.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court lacks jurisdiction over a claim against the government concerning its order affecting land granted or held as a Saranjam.
material_facts: The claimant sought a finding that the government’s order granting the properties to another person was invalid and did not affect the properties.
The claimant also sought possession of the properties despite that order.
The properties were maintenance holdings within a Saranjam, and the government was therefore more than a formal party to the claim.
issues.conclusion: The claim against the government concerning its order over Saranjam lands was barred from determination by the civil court under section 4 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(a), fourth sub-clause, of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876, excludes civil-court jurisdiction over claims against the government relating to lands granted or held as a Saranjam. The Court applied the distinction between claims and suits discussed in Mallappa alias Annasaheb Basvantrao Desai Nadgouda v. Tukkao Narshinha Mutalik Desai and Others.

predicates.saranjam_land_jurisdiction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal involving a civil-court claim concerning land held as a Saranjam.
predicates.claimant_challenges_government_order_aff: The claimant asks the court to invalidate or disregard a government order affecting Saranjam land.
predicates.possession_claim_depends_on_invalidating: The claimant’s request for possession depends on the court setting aside or disregarding the government order.

issues.definition: A civil court lacks jurisdiction over a government-related claim concerning Saranjam land when the claimant’s request for possession depends on invalidating or disregarding the government’s order affecting that land.
